nameStory: The 'tall tumblemustard' gets its memorable name from its impressive height and its dramatic end-of-life performance. After the plant matures and dries out, it breaks free from its roots and tumbles across the landscape like a classic Western tumbleweed, scattering seeds as it rolls. It's also called 'Jim Hill mustard' after the famous railroad baron, since it often spreads along railway corridors.
description: Tall tumblemustard is a towering annual herb in the mustard family that can reach impressive heights of 3-6 feet or more. This European native has deeply divided, feathery leaves and produces clusters of small yellow flowers that develop into long, thin seed pods. The plant starts as a low rosette but quickly shoots up into a tall, branched stem that eventually becomes the classic tumbleweed we see rolling across open areas.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely tall for a mustard plant, often towering 3-6 feet high with many branching stems that create an open, airy appearance when mature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into narrow, feathery segments that feel somewhat rough to the touch, with the lowest leaves forming a rosette early in the season

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale yellow flowers with four petals arranged in loose clusters along the branching stems, each flower only about 1/8 inch across

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Very long, thin seed pods (2-4 inches) that stick out at angles from the stem and split open to reveal small brown seeds

idTips.label: Mature Form
idTips.description: When dried, the entire plant becomes brittle and tan-colored, breaking away at ground level to form the classic spherical tumbleweed

habitat: In New England, this rare visitor is most likely found in disturbed areas like roadsides, railroad tracks, vacant lots, and construction sites. It prefers dry, sandy or gravelly soils and full sun exposure. Given its extremely limited presence in our region (only one recorded observation), it's more of a chance encounter than a reliable find.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of deeply divided leaves, staying low to the ground initially.
seasonality.summer: Rapid upward growth occurs with flowering from June through August, when the characteristic tall, branching structure develops.
seasonality.fall: Plants dry out and turn brown, eventually breaking free to become tumbleweeds that may persist into winter.
seasonality.winter: Dead, dried stems may remain standing or the entire plant may have broken away and blown elsewhere.

funFact: This plant is essentially a biological pinball machine - when it becomes a tumbleweed, a single plant can scatter up to 100,000 seeds across miles of landscape, with some tumbleweeds documented traveling over 100 miles from their birthplace!
confusionNotes: Its impressive height distinguishes it from most other mustard family plants in New England, but it could be confused with other tall weedy plants when not in flower. Look for the characteristic deeply divided, feathery leaves and the long, thin seed pods that angle out from the stems - these are classic mustard family features.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'mustard,' this plant is quite different from the common yellow mustard we put on hot dogs, though they are related. The tumbleweed behavior is actually quite rare among New England plants - most of our native species have evolved different seed dispersal strategies suited to our forested landscape rather than open plains.
compareHints: Tall tumblemustard lives up to its name by growing much taller than its relatives like hedge mustard, which typically stays under 3 feet. Unlike false London-rocket, tall tumblemustard has more finely divided, feathery leaves and develops the distinctive tumbleweed form when mature. The extreme height and eventual tumbling behavior make it quite distinctive among the hedgemustards.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hedge mustard differs from its relatives False London-rocket and Tall Tumblemustard primarily in its seed pod arrangement and overall size.
Compared to its close relative Hedge Mustard, False London-rocket grows much taller and has more finely divided, feathery leaves rather than the broader, less-divided leaves of Hedge Mustard.
